tldr: This paper mathematically unifies five key design decisions in robot imitation learning—model capacity, data collection, representations, optimization, and deployment—under a single conditional predictive distribution target. It reveals the exact effects of each intervention and uncovers pitfalls in common evaluation metrics without relying on uncertain scaling laws.
hero_caption: Five interconnected training design choices linked under a single Behavior Cloning objective: (1) coupling of model capacity and data volume, (2) data collection aligned with evaluation priorities, (3) preventing information loss from representations and preserving policy expressiveness, (4) tuning optimization convergence, and (5) contextual weighting during real-world deployment.
overview:
When training robot policies with Behavior Cloning (BC), we constantly face the dilemma of where to allocate our limited compute and data budgets next. Questions like "Should we collect more demonstrations or scale the model?", "Which pretrained representation should we choose?", and "Why did test loss go down while real-robot performance got worse?" are typically answered using rules of thumb or empirical scaling laws.

This paper proposes a framework that unifies these seemingly disjoint design decisions under a single common target: predicting the expert's conditional action distribution in a fixed reference environment. By establishing a hierarchy of nested learning oracles, the authors decompose imitation risk and derive exact mathematical relationships across five design axes—capacity, data allocation, representation, optimization, and deployment—using local information geometry, conditional mutual information, and optimization theory (Polyak–Łojasiewicz conditions).

The theoretical predictions are validated through analytically solvable Gaussian models, discrete counterexamples, and geometric analyses across 206 public trajectories from the PushT benchmark. These experiments clearly expose capacity–data coupling, representation-induced mixture mismatch, and an metric-reversal phenomenon where deployment imitation error (KL divergence) increases even as test loss (negative log-likelihood) decreases due to shifts in conditional entropy.

A key strength of this work is showing how the geometric properties of data and representations can be quantified before training any policy. It provides practical, mathematically grounded guidelines for budgeting resources and avoiding the deceptive traps of seemingly favorable predictive metrics.
contributions: Unified five resource-allocation decisions in robot behavior cloning (capacity, data allocation, representation, optimization, and deployment) under a single conditional predictive target, deriving an exact risk accounting framework and mathematical relations.

Mathematically proved that state compression via pretrained representations alters the effective conditional distribution seen by the learner (representation-induced mixture mismatch), even when the underlying expert remains unchanged.

Demonstrated a concrete sign-reversal phenomenon where negative log-likelihood (NLL) improves while imitation error (KL divergence) deteriorates due to differences in conditional entropy between deployment and training environments.

Evaluated an information-design criterion that determines optimal data collection allocations using only the Fisher information geometry of state features on the PushT dataset, without fitting any policy.

sections.heading: Untangling Resource Allocation in Imitation Learning with a Single Target
sections.summary: Robot behavior cloning involves complex trade-offs across data collection, encoder choice, model capacity, and optimization. This paper organizes these decisions around a fixed, common expert prediction target to provide clear guidance on where to invest the next unit of resources.
sections.details:
Resource allocation in robot Behavior Cloning (BC) is a challenging puzzle. The same amount of data may carry vastly different amounts of actionable information. Different feature encoders with identical output dimensions preserve completely different geometric cues. Moreover, clean loss convergence does not guarantee that you have learned a working policy. What researchers and engineers really need is a principled criterion to decide where to invest the next marginal unit of data or compute—whether into model scaling, data collection, better representations, or optimization.

This work anchors all these choices to a single conditional probability target: predicting expert actions from past history, $p(a \mid h)$, where histories combine images, language, proprioception, and contact signals. By keeping this target fixed, the authors connect five core design dimensions—Capacity, Acquisition (data), Representation, Optimization, and Deployment—without conflating their underlying assumptions.

The authors introduce a framework that cleanly separates imitation risk from approximation and optimization errors. Through rigorous proofs, analytically solvable numerical checks, and an information-design analysis on PushT trajectory data, the paper clarifies exactly under what conditions each intervention produces genuine gains.

captions.F1: Five learning design decisions linked under a common behavior cloning objective. Task space and camera setups are shown alongside PCA visualizations across layers of ResNet-50, CLIP, and DINOv2, intuitively illustrating how different pretrained representations preserve distinctly different geometric information.

sections.heading: Fixing the Target and Strictly Accounting for Risk
sections.summary: Defining imitation risk as the KL divergence to the expert's conditional action distribution enables a strict decomposition into data, representation, optimization, and distribution-shift gaps using nested oracles. It also clarifies the crucial difference between negative log-likelihood and KL divergence.
sections.details:
The paper first builds the formal mathematical foundation. Let $H$ denote histories and $A$ denote actions. An unknown expert $\xi$ induces a conditional distribution $p_\xi(a \mid h)$ over a reference history distribution $d_{E,\xi}$. Imitation risk $\mathcal{R}_E(\pi)$ is defined as the expected KL divergence between the expert and the learned policy $\pi$.

The standard predictive training loss, negative log-likelihood (NLL) $C_E(\pi)$, splits into the expert's conditional entropy $\mathsf{H}_E(A \mid H)$ plus the imitation risk: $C_E(\pi) = \mathsf{H}_E(A \mid H) + \mathcal{R}_E(\pi)$. When comparing two policies on the exact same fixed target, the difference in NLL equals the difference in imitation risk without needing to know the entropy. However, the absolute value of NLL is only a predictive score, not the absolute KL divergence. In closed-loop deployment, an agent's own actions shift the visited history distribution, so offline predictive performance and closed-loop task success are fundamentally distinct.

To account for risk under finite budgets, the authors introduce a hierarchy of nested learning oracles:
- $L^{(0)}$: Best risk achievable with infinite data, ideal representations, and exact optimization
- $L^{(1)}$: Best risk achievable under a finite dataset $D$
- $L^{(2)}$: Best risk achievable through a specific feature representation $g$
- $L^{(3)}$: Risk of the policy learned under an algorithm and capacity constraint $N$
- $L_{\rm dep}$: Risk encountered in the actual deployment environment

Total risk decomposes into four non-overlapping components: the data gap $\Delta_{\rm data} = L^{(1)} - L^{(0)}$, the representation gap $\Delta_{\rm repr} = L^{(2)} - L^{(1)}$, the algorithmic/capacity gap $\Delta_{\rm alg} = L^{(3)} - L^{(2)}$, and the deployment distribution shift $\Delta_{\rm shift} = L_{\rm dep} - L^{(3)}$. Because each step adds constraints, the infimum cannot decrease, ensuring the first three terms are always non-negative ($\ge 0$).

sections.heading: Five Conditional Training Relations: The Math Behind Resource Trade-Offs
sections.summary: The authors derive five concrete relations governing capacity vs. data, target-weighted data allocation, representation vs. policy expressiveness, optimization vs. generalization, and deployment contexts. These equations reveal how each intervention interacts with the others and where bottlenecks emerge.
sections.details:
Building on the risk decomposition, the authors derive explicit mathematical relations governing each design axis:

### 3.1 Capacity and data
In standard power-law scaling models $a N^{-\alpha} + c D^{-\beta}$ under a fixed compute budget $F = \kappa N D$, the optimal balance is not found by simply equating the two terms (crossover). Instead, it requires matching their weighted marginal returns: $\alpha a N^{-\alpha} = \beta c D^{-\beta}$. Furthermore, in an analytically solvable Gaussian prior model, the Bayes risk couples capacity $N$ and data size $D$ into inseparable terms (a sum of $\frac{\sigma^2}{D} \frac{\tau_j^4}{\tau_j^2 + \sigma^2/D}$), proving that capacity and data cannot always be neatly disentangled.

### 3.2 Target-weighted data allocation
When the input space is partitioned into strata, the value of each stratum depends on how its Fisher information $F_i$ aligns with the evaluation Hessian $G_E$. Adding a sample $n_i$ provides marginal utility $v_i = \operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{I}^{-1} F_i \mathcal{I}^{-1} G_E)$, where $\mathcal{I} = \sum n_i F_i$. Optimal allocation equalizes the ratio $v_i / c_i$ relative to collection cost $c_i$. Data that fills in information along directions prioritized by evaluation carries higher value.

### 3.3 Representation and policy expressiveness
When histories $H$ are compressed into features $Z = g(H)$, imitation risk is lower-bounded by $I(A; H \mid Z) + \inf_\pi \mathbb{E}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p(A \mid Z) \| \pi(A \mid Z))]$. The first term is the conditional mutual information discarded by the encoder; the second term reflects the policy head's limited expressiveness. No matter how large the policy head is, information lost in the first term can never be recovered. Crucially, with a lossy encoder, simply altering data sampling proportions shifts the effective target distribution $p(A \mid Z)$ seen by the head (representation-induced mixture mismatch), even if the underlying $p(A \mid H)$ has not changed.

### 3.4 Optimization and generalization
If the loss surface satisfies $L_s$-smoothness and the Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) condition, gradient descent drives optimization error down exponentially with step count. However, sampling uncertainty (uniform deviation $u_S$) always persists between empirical and expected risk. Pushing optimization error toward zero cannot overcome this sample-size error floor.

### 3.5 Deployment contexts
When the deployment history distribution $d_{\rm dep}$ differs from the evaluation distribution $d_E$, the shift in imitation risk depends on the covariance $\operatorname{Cov}_{d_E}(w, \ell_\pi)$ between importance weights $w = d_{\rm dep} / d_E$ and local imitation loss $\ell_\pi(h)$. If the policy happens to perform well on frequently visited deployment contexts, risk drops; otherwise, it spikes. Furthermore, because NLL incorporates shifting conditional entropy, deployment NLL can drop even while KL divergence worsens.

sections.heading: Numerical Sanity Checks: Exposing Metric Traps in Known Models
sections.summary: To confirm the theoretical relations, the authors ran numerical checks on analytically tractable Gaussian models and discrete distributions. The simulations matched theoretical values with extreme precision and confirmed the counterintuitive case where NLL decreases while KL divergence gets worse.
sections.details:
To verify that the theoretical derivations hold quantitatively, the authors performed numerical checks on toy models with known ground-truth distributions.

First, they tested an $m=16$ dimensional Gaussian model with power-law decaying prior variance ($\tau_j^2 = j^{-1.3}$). Across configurations with capacity $N \in \{2, 8, 16\}$ and data size $D \in \{4, 16, 64, 256\}$, results from 100,000 Monte Carlo trials matched exact theoretical Bayes risks within a relative deviation of at most 0.14% (within 1.25 standard errors), validating the coupled capacity–data formula.

Next, they analyzed representation compression and distribution shifts using a discrete 4-context Bernoulli model. Pairing contexts into two composite states (feature reduction) introduced an irrecoverable information loss of 0.05123 nats. Even when expert action probabilities were identical across contexts, varying sampling proportions altered the optimal conditional target over the compressed features, demonstrating persistent representation-induced mismatch.

Most strikingly, shifting the evaluation distribution revealed a sharp metric reversal: for a fixed policy, changing the target distribution caused imitation error (KL divergence) to degrade by +0.04200 nats, while predictive loss (NLL) dropped by -0.06495 nats—appearing to improve. This discrepancy is explained by a concurrent drop in environmental conditional entropy of -0.10695 nats. Comparing raw NLL values across different distributions without accounting for entropy changes can completely mislead conclusions about imitation quality.

sections.heading: Information Geometry on Public PushT Trajectories
sections.summary: Without training any policy, the authors evaluated data allocation criteria purely using the Fisher information geometry of state features on the public PushT dataset. Under asymmetric target distributions, information-guided allocation reduced the design criterion by 4.5% to 6.2% compared to target matching.
sections.details:
To evaluate whether information-design criteria work on real robotic trajectories, the authors analyzed the PushT task available in LeRobot (a simulated T-block pushing task with 206 episodes and 25,650 steps). Remarkably, **no neural network policy was trained for this analysis**.

### Experimental Setup
The dataset was partitioned into 144 calibration episodes and 62 evaluation episodes. The state space was split into two horizontal strata at pusher coordinate $x=256$. Over normalized coordinates, they computed second-order polynomial features $\phi = (1, x, y, xy, x^2, y^2)$ (and first-order $\phi=(1,x,y)$ for sensitivity checks). The average outer-product matrix $\widehat{F}_{s,i} = \mathbb{E}[\phi \phi^\top]$ served as the Fisher information in a linear-Gaussian setting to evaluate the regularized design criterion $V(q)$ across target weights $w \in \{0.2, 0.5, 0.8\}$.

### Key Findings
Optimal sampling allocations $\hat{q}$ computed on calibration data were evaluated on unseen test data against three baselines: balanced sampling ($q=0.5$), target matching ($q=w$), and the empirical dataset proportion ($q=0.5736$).

- Under asymmetric evaluation weights ($w=0.2$ and $w=0.8$), the optimal allocation settled between balanced sampling and target matching, reducing the design criterion by **6.23%** and **4.93%** respectively for second-order features compared to target matching.
- Under symmetric evaluation weights ($w=0.5$), the reduction was essentially zero (0.00% for second-order, and -0.03% for first-order), showing no benefit over uniform collection.
- The optimal allocation differed between first-order and second-order features, demonstrating that optimal data collection is tightly coupled to the chosen representation.

All estimates accounted for temporal correlations across consecutive steps using episode-level block bootstrap confidence intervals.

sections.heading: Discussion: Why Assumptions Matter and the Scope of This Framework
sections.summary: The five training relations are not isolated additive effects; they are tightly coupled. The authors discuss the critical need to distinguish local geometric regimes from bias-dominated regimes and emphasize declaring what is held fixed versus what is varied during interventions.
sections.details:
The authors emphasize that these five relations interact dynamically rather than acting in isolation. For instance, the optimal data collection allocation depends directly on the encoder's representation (information matrix), and compressing representations distorts the predictive target faced by the policy head. Practitioners must clearly define what is held fixed and what is allowed to vary when evaluating any training intervention.

Furthermore, the PushT analysis demonstrates that collecting data in exact proportion to deployment frequencies is not always optimal from an information-geometric perspective. However, if a model suffers from severe underparameterization (bias), incomplete optimization, or feature aliasing, those defects will quickly overshadow any geometric benefits from optimal data allocation.

### Limitations and Scope
The theory comes with concrete assumptions and boundaries:
- Finite-description capacity bounds do not fully capture the expressive properties of unconstrained deep networks.
- Local Fisher information approximations can fail when models are severely misspecified or encounter singular geometries.
- The PushT validation relies on handcrafted features in a single-task simulation; it does not directly evaluate language conditioning or cross-embodiment generalization typical of modern Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.
- Because evaluations reweight fixed policies, they do not directly model closed-loop distribution drift caused by compounding policy errors over time.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Pinpoint the Bottleneck and Measure Interventions Accurately
sections.summary: Anchoring analysis to a common conditional distribution turns vague discussions about scaling into precise resource-allocation problems. Rather than blindly following empirical scaling laws, practitioners should diagnose active bottlenecks and select the right metrics for their interventions.
sections.details:
This study places several intuitive heuristics in physical action model training onto a firm mathematical foundation.

Capacity and data volume are fundamentally coupled. The value of demonstration data depends on both task target priorities and state geometry. Representation-induced information loss cannot be compensated for by scaling the policy head, and training loss convergence does not guarantee deployment robustness. As highlighted by the sign reversal between NLL and KL divergence, surface-level predictive metrics can easily mislead practitioners about actual control performance.

The authors' final recipe is practical and principled: diagnose where your training pipeline's current bottleneck lies, clearly declare what assumptions are held fixed, and measure interventions using mathematically appropriate metrics.

takeaways: Comparing test NLL across different distributions is dangerous: shifts in environmental conditional entropy can cause NLL to look better even as imitation error (KL divergence) gets worse.

Encoder information loss cannot be fixed by expanding the policy head: information discarded during compression becomes a permanent error floor $I(A; H \mid Z)$ and distorts the effective target distribution depending on sampling ratios.

Matching data collection to test-time frequencies is not always optimal: allocating samples toward information-rich strata can improve geometric design criteria over target matching (by 4.5% to 6.2% on PushT).

Endless optimization cannot break through the generalization floor: even if empirical loss converges exponentially under the PL condition, finite-sample uncertainty $u_S$ sets an insurmountable lower bound.
limitations: No direct verification of closed-loop success rates: The findings focus on theoretical risk and state-space geometry rather than measuring task completion rates on real hardware.

Evaluations are limited to fixed features and a single task: The PushT validation uses simple polynomial features on a single simulated task, leaving open direct evaluations on large pretrained vision encoders or multi-task VLA models.

Trajectory-level collection constraints are omitted: Even if an optimal sampling ratio across state strata is known, collecting continuous robot trajectories that respect those exact ratios in practice remains an open operational challenge.
